title: The enemy as teacher
hookLine: nobody gets strong lifting an empty bar; Shantideva calls the person who wrongs him a treasure found at home
tomorrow: someone else gets the praise you wanted. can you be glad?

cards: Ask anyone who lifts weights: the bar is what makes you strong. Nobody builds anything lifting an empty bar. The weight that pushes back is the whole point.
Patience works the same way, and that's the answer to yesterday's question. If nobody ever tested you, where would patience come from?
Shantideva says it outright, and then he says something that sounds almost outrageous about the people who wrong us.

teach.b: Without someone who wrongs me, he asks, where would I practice patience?
So that person is like a treasure that turns up in my own house without any effort, helping me on the path to awakening. He should be cherished.
This doesn't excuse harm, and it doesn't ask anyone to stay where they're hurt. Shantideva is clear that the person had no intention of helping. The gift is in what you make of the moment.
Now the week, in six lines. Like a log: still as wood while the fire's going. Check first: a glance inward before moving.
A boat, not an idol: the body, cared for and used. One flash burns much: notice the shimmer in the pan. Why worry: act on what can be fixed, release what can't.
What moved them: the hand, and the anger behind it.
And today's, which ties chapter six's start together: the hard person in front of you is my teacher of patience.

how: In Tibetan mind-training (lojong) and in teachings on patience, Buddhists are encouraged to regard difficult people as teachers of patience, while still protecting themselves and others from harm.

games.q: what does “the enemy as teacher” mean?
o: a strict teacher who punishes every mistake you make
a rival you study closely so you can beat them later
seeing a difficult person as a chance to grow patience

games.q: the week's lines — tap the pairs.
p: still as wood while the fire burns
act on what can be fixed
the one who gives you the chance

s: seeing someone as a teacher of patience means staying where you're harmed
it doesn't excuse harm or ask anyone to stay; the gift is what you make of the moment.
Shantideva compares the one who wrongs him to a treasure found at home
found without effort, helping him on the path to awakening.

games.q: your new manager micromanages every email you send, and it's driving you up the wall. what does 'enemy as teacher' look like this week?
o: use each check-in to practice not snapping, and still ask for more trust.
thank her loudly, so she sees how patient you're being with her.
say nothing and accept it forever, since she's your teacher now.
games.why: the hard person is the weight on the bar. Shantideva's patience grows in the moment, and it doesn't mean giving up a fair request.

practice: Bring to mind one person who's been hard to deal with lately, not someone who has truly harmed you.

On your phone or on paper, version a short note thanking them for one thing they taught you, even unwillingly, like waiting, or not snapping back. You don't have to send it; just let the words sit there while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: The enemy as teacher: Shantideva's turn in chapter six. The one who wrongs you gives you the chance to practice patience.

orig.note: Sanskrit: patience, forbearance; the subject of chapter six. Pali khanti.

carryVoice: The line to keep: my teacher of patience, said quietly, not to excuse anything. Two weeks with Shantideva, complete.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 6.105-6.111 (without one who wrongs me, there is no chance for patience; the enemy is like a treasure appearing in my house without effort, helping my practice of awakening; he has no intention to help, yet the chance is real)
